title: Comcast store punished low sales by smashing pies in workers' faces, lawsuit claims
gist: A Connecticut lawsuit alleges a Comcast store manager in Plainville ran a monthly ritual in which the top-ranked sales consultant tied the lowest-ranked one to a chair and smashed a cream pie in their face, with the assaults videotaped and tracked on a back-office chart, allegedly to drive sales and survey scores. Comcast disputes the claims; the negligence theory turns on failure to supervise store management.

insights.claim: The complaint alleges a Comcast store in Plainville, Connecticut had a policy where the prior month's highest-ranked Retail Sales Consultant was instructed by store manager Sully Fuentes Peterson to tie the lowest-ranked consultant to a chair in the back office and smash a cream pie in their face.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Allegations of physical coercion embedded in a sales-incentive structure are the kind of frontline-management failure that generates outsized reputational and legal cost relative to the store's revenue.
insights.locator: A Comcast store in Plainville, Connecticut

insights.claim: Plaintiff David Figueroa alleges Peterson designed and implemented the ritual specifically to meet goals related to sales and positive customer survey responses.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Ties the alleged misconduct directly to corporate performance metrics—the link plaintiffs need to reach past the individual manager to the company.
insights.locator: Figueroa alleges that Peterson “designed and implemented”

insights.claim: Peterson allegedly maintained a back-office chart ranking sales staff and identifying employees who had been recently assaulted or were scheduled to be, with the complaint including a photo showing first names, a month, and a pie-face emoji.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Documentary evidence created by the alleged perpetrator is the strongest category of proof—raises settlement probability substantially.
insights.locator: Peterson maintained a chart in the back office

insights.claim: The lawsuit alleges the assaults were videotaped by Peterson, that she ordered staff to participate and record their own videos, and that Figueroa himself witnessed and videotaped a coworker named Ty being tied up and assaulted.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Video evidence and forced participation implicate multiple witnesses—expands potential plaintiff pool beyond the named claimant.
insights.quote: assaults were videotaped by Ms. Peterson

insights.claim: A separate alleged incident involved an assistant sales manager named Jania being pied because she received a poor survey score from a customer, with Figueroa viewing the video on a coworker's phone.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Extension of the practice to management-level staff and to survey scores suggests a systematic practice rather than an isolated event.
insights.locator: The lawsuit alleges that in another incident

insights.claim: Figueroa was hired February 2, 2026 and resigned February 27, alleging constructive discharge because a reasonable person in his position would have felt compelled to resign given the atmosphere of pervasive threats and actual violence.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A 25-day tenure makes economic damages small but constructive discharge and emotional distress claims carry the case—reputational cost exceeds financial exposure.

insights.claim: The negligence theory is that Comcast reasonably should have known about store management's policies and failed to properly supervise the store management team, allowing employees to be humiliated for the purpose of promoting revenues and profits.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Failure-to-supervise is the standard vehicle for reaching corporate defendants over franchise or store-level conduct—the outcome depends on what escalation records show.
insights.locator: The lawsuit says the defendant, Comcast, was negligent

insights.claim: Figueroa says he called Comcast regional manager Maranda Cody on February 27 to report the assaults, was told to memorialize his concerns in a text message, and never received a response before resigning.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: An unanswered escalation to regional management is precisely the fact pattern that converts individual misconduct into corporate liability.
insights.locator: Figueroa’s lawsuit said that on February 27

insights.claim: The lawsuit alleges Comcast did not disclose the pie-assault policy to Figueroa before he accepted the job offer, framing it as an undisclosed condition of employment.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The non-disclosure framing supports the constructive discharge theory by establishing the practice was not a known term of employment.
insights.locator: Defendant did not inform the Plaintiff prior to his acceptance

insights.claim: Comcast said it disagrees with the claims and their characterization, cited zero tolerance for harassment or humiliation, declined to comment on specifics, and would not say whether it still employs the manager.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Refusing to confirm the manager's employment status is the notable omission—usually signals an unresolved internal situation.
insights.quote: The Company has zero tolerance for harassment, humiliation, or any behavior that compromises a respectful and safe workplace,
insights.locator: Comcast provided a statement to Ars today

insights.claim: The complaint was filed July 9 in a Connecticut superior court and seeks compensatory damages for past and future economic losses and emotional distress.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: State-court compensatory-only claims are modest in dollar terms—this is a reputational story, not a material financial one for Comcast.

themes.theme: Business context behind the sales pressure

insights.claim: Comcast's cable division has spent the past year trying to reverse customer losses by offering a five-year price guarantee and plans without data caps.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Multi-year price guarantees to stem subscriber losses compress ARPU and margin—the retention cost of a structurally declining cable business.
insights.locator: Comcast’s cable division has been trying to reverse customer losses

insights.claim: Those changes followed Comcast President Mike Cavanagh's April 2025 statement that the company is not winning in the marketplace.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Executive-level acknowledgment of competitive loss provides the pressure context in which extreme store-level sales tactics allegedly emerged.
insights.quote: we are not winning in the marketplace
insights.locator: The changes came after Comcast President Mike Cavanagh said
